title: Moskow expects slower US spending to make room for stronger exports
summary: Chicago Fed President Michael Moskow's 12 January outlook required two things to happen together. Higher long-term rates would slow US household and business spending, while recovery overseas would bring more orders to US producers. In 1999 domestic spending had risen about 5%, roughly a percentage point faster than real GDP. The difference was partly absorbed by rising imports and a widening trade deficit financed by investment from abroad. If the deficit stopped widening in 2000, an equivalent increase in domestic spending would place greater pressure on US production. Moskow expected moderation at home to make enough room for the change abroad. His forecast was real GDP growth of about 3½% from the fourth quarter of 1999 to the fourth quarter of 2000, with year-end unemployment roughly stable.

The forecast incorporated a sizeable reassessment of supply. An economy that economists had recently expected could sustain 2–2½% growth now seemed capable of around 3½%, combining workforce growth of about 1% with productivity growth of about 2½%. Average annual productivity growth over the past four years had exceeded its pace over the preceding quarter-century by about a percentage point. Moskow also noted that around half a percentage point of the upward revision to sustainable growth reflected changes in how the Commerce Department measured GDP. An estimate formed using the old accounts should therefore be compared carefully with observations under the newer definition. He also saw signs that staffing intermediaries and a more flexible labour market had improved job matching. Unemployment had averaged 4.2% in 1999, making an earlier rule of thumb that trouble would start around 6% hard to defend.

Moskow separated the rate-sensitive component of business investment from the portion justified by high prospective returns on technology. Investment in equipment, software and structures had increased almost 10% in 1999. He expected higher long rates to curb its growth, while falling equipment prices and the opportunity to install applications postponed during preparation for the date change would support technology purchases. There is a distinction between postponing a particular application and forecasting a contraction in overall technology investment. His expectation was slower growth in business investment alongside continued rapid technology spending. Such investment also affects future supply, whereas orders placed today first register as demand.

Households presented a larger test because their spending represented about two thirds of real GDP and had grown roughly 5% in 1999. Existing-home sales and light-vehicle purchases had hit records. US light-vehicle sales had reached 16.8 million, particularly important to Midwest manufacturing. Moskow judged that housing activity appeared to have peaked around mid-1999, and expected higher rates and the difficulty of repeating a record sales year to restrain housing, autos and other durables. But near-record consumer confidence in December, rising real incomes and gains in stock and housing wealth favoured continued spending. Home financing had also supported households' spending power in the first half of 1999. A normalisation in durables could therefore coexist with resilient total consumption.

The international forecast amplified the significance of those household and investment calls. Recovery in Asia and South America, faster growth in Western Europe and healthy demand from Canada and Mexico should accelerate US exports. Slower domestic spending should temper import growth. Moskow consequently expected the trade deficit to widen little, if at all, after two years of large increases. This forecast concerned the change in the deficit. A sizeable deficit could persist even as net trade ceased to take as much away from GDP growth. The risk was that overseas orders would recover as expected while US consumption stayed closer to its previous pace, leaving American producers short of capacity despite better productivity.

Two inflation measures could then move in different directions. Chicago's estimate put 1999 headline CPI inflation at 2.6%, up from 1.5% in 1998, primarily because of oil. Moskow expected lower headline inflation in 2000 because energy prices were unlikely to repeat their previous rise, but a modest increase in core CPI inflation. Earlier rises in energy costs could pass through to other prices. Employers' health benefit costs were picking up and the prior decline in import prices had ended. A lower headline reading consequently offered limited evidence on its own that underlying pressure was easing. The speech gives directional forecasts for both indices and a growth rate for GDP. It does not give a target for the federal funds rate or a market reaction to the forecast.

Moskow's concern was a shrinking pool of available workers even with substantially better output per worker. He also stressed how sustained expansion gave workers entering late in the cycle time to build experience and income. For the historical record, that helps explain why he accepted growth well above the earlier estimate of potential while still worrying about excess demand. The next test was whether private spending slowed enough as exports strengthened and whether employers could absorb rising costs while continuing to hire.

questions.question: Did US domestic demand moderate enough to offset recovery in foreign orders?
questions.detail: Reconstruct the quarterly contributions of consumption, business investment, exports and imports using the GDP vintages available at the time. Compare fourth-quarter-to-fourth-quarter GDP growth with Moskow's 3½% projection. A smaller drag from net trade alongside broadly slower household spending would validate his composition call even if total growth differed modestly. Weaker imports caused by a contraction in domestic demand would imply a very different outlook.

questions.question: Which rate-sensitive purchases slowed first, and how much did asset wealth or technology investment offset that slowing?
questions.detail: Look at mortgage rates, home transactions, vehicle sales and financing, equipment orders and software spending in sequence. Compare Midwest motor-vehicle manufacturing with national retail sales and stocks of unsold cars. An inventory correction following 1999's record can lower production without an equivalent fall in final sales. Sustained technology orders despite higher long rates would support Moskow's distinction between financing costs and expected investment returns.

questions.question: Could headline inflation ease while the underlying cost trend strengthened enough to affect monetary policy?
questions.detail: Separate energy's direct contribution to CPI from changes in core CPI components, import prices, employment benefits and unit labour costs. Track whether industries with greater exposure to energy inputs were the first to raise prices. Broad, repeated increases outside those sectors alongside stronger pay per unit of output would be a different policy signal from a one-off pass-through of oil costs.
